reconcile.note: The Geneva annotators read the command to choose life as an obedience that God's Spirit itself works in the elect, folding the summons into election rather than against it.

discrepancy.note: Ingersoll argues that divine decrees of predestination and damnation abolish moral freedom, reducing choice to grim necessity.

quotes.text: If this be the end of all philosophy, it is equally the end of "all things." Not only does it make an end of us and of our hopes of futurity, but of all that makes the present life worth living—of all freedom, and hence of all virtue.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (Ingersoll's Rejoinder to Judge Jeremiah S. Black) (1881), on Deuteronomy 30:19 and Romans 9:18.

quotes.text: You cannot find words sufficient to express your horror of the doctrine of Divine decrees; and yet here you have decrees with a vengeance—predestination and damnation, both in one.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (Ingersoll's Rejoinder to Judge Jeremiah S. Black) (1881), on Deuteronomy 30:19 and Romans 9:18.

sides.snippet: I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse: therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your seed;
sides.verseText: I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse: therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your seed;

sides.snippet: So then, he has mercy on whom he desires, and he hardens whom he desires.
sides.verseText: So then, he has mercy on whom he desires, and he hardens whom he desires.
